questions.nclexClientNeeds: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
questions.question: Which statement best distinguishes colonization from infection?
choices: Colonization means organisms are present without symptoms or tissue invasion, while infection causes invasion and a host response
Colonization always requires antimicrobial treatment
Infection can occur only when a blood culture is positive
Colonized clients cannot transmit organisms
questions.explanation: Colonized people carry organisms without symptomatic tissue invasion but may still transmit them. Infection reflects invasion, multiplication, and a clinical or tissue response; results require context.

questions.nclexClientNeeds: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
questions.question: Which nursing action most directly interrupts a mode of transmission in the chain of infection?
choices: Performing hand hygiene before and after client contact
Increasing the microorganism's virulence
Creating a new portal of entry
Suppressing the client's immune response
questions.explanation: Hand hygiene reduces transfer of organisms by contact and interrupts transmission. Infection prevention can also target the reservoir, portals of exit and entry, or host susceptibility.

questions.question: Why might the same microorganism cause colonization in one client and invasive infection in another?
choices: Disease depends only on the organism's name
Virulence, inoculum, portal of entry and host defenses interact
Every exposure produces an identical response
Vaccination eliminates all differences in susceptibility
questions.explanation: Clinical outcome reflects both microbial features and host factors, including barrier integrity, immune status, devices, chronic illness, exposure dose, and route of entry.

questions.question: Which feature of an indwelling device can support persistent or recurrent infection?
choices: A biofilm that protects an attached microbial community
Permanent sterilization by body fluids
Conversion of bacteria into platelets
Elimination of every portal of entry
questions.explanation: Microorganisms can form a protective biofilm on devices and damaged tissue, limiting immune clearance and antimicrobial penetration. Avoiding unnecessary devices reduces this risk.

questions.question: Blood cultures and an urgent first dose of antimicrobial are ordered for an unstable client with suspected sepsis. What should the RN do?
choices: Delay all treatment until the final culture report
Obtain the ordered cultures promptly when feasible without delaying time-critical therapy
Collect cultures after several doses regardless of timing
Cancel cultures because antimicrobials were prescribed
questions.explanation: Cultures are ideally collected before antimicrobials when this can be done promptly, but emergency stabilization and time-critical treatment must not be delayed solely for specimen collection.

questions.question: Which action best supports antimicrobial stewardship after culture and susceptibility results return?
choices: Continue the broadest therapy indefinitely
Collaborate to narrow or stop therapy when clinical evidence and results support it
Save remaining doses for a future illness
Share the prescription with a family member who has similar symptoms
questions.explanation: Stewardship uses the appropriate agent, dose, route, and duration and reassesses broad therapy when evidence becomes available. Clients should never save or share prescribed antimicrobials.

questions.question: Which statement about bacteremia and sepsis is correct?
choices: They are interchangeable terms
Bacteremia is bacteria in blood, while sepsis is a life-threatening systemic response to infection with organ dysfunction
Sepsis requires a positive blood culture
Transient bacteremia always causes shock
questions.explanation: Bacteremia describes viable bacteria in the bloodstream and may be transient or serious. Sepsis is defined by a dangerous systemic response and organ dysfunction and may occur without positive cultures.

questions.question: Which cue cluster most strongly suggests infection-related organ dysfunction rather than an uncomplicated local infection?
choices: Small area of tenderness with stable vital signs
New confusion, tachypnea, falling blood pressure and decreased urine output
Positive screening swab without symptoms
Mild itching beneath an adhesive
questions.explanation: Acute neurologic, respiratory, perfusion, and renal changes suggest systemic deterioration and possible sepsis. This cluster requires immediate assessment and protocol-based escalation.

questions.question: A client with suspected infection is confused, hypotensive and tachypneic but has no fever. What is the priority nursing action?
choices: Wait for fever before reporting the findings
Assess ABCs and perfusion and activate the appropriate emergency or sepsis pathway
Give an antipyretic and reassess tomorrow
Assume confusion is an expected effect of aging
questions.explanation: Sepsis can occur without fever. Suspected infection plus new organ-function and perfusion changes requires immediate stabilization, escalation, timely treatment, and repeated reassessment.

questions.question: Which finding best supports improvement after treatment for systemic infection?
choices: Temperature falls briefly after an antipyretic while blood pressure continues to fall
Mental status, perfusion, urine output and work of breathing improve together
One inflammatory marker declines while oxygen need rises
Pain worsens despite a normal white blood cell count
questions.explanation: Improvement should appear across clinically meaningful trends, especially organ function and perfusion. A single temperature or laboratory change cannot outweigh worsening respiratory or circulatory status.
